claim: CD81 was identified as one of the altered proteins upon CD44 depletion in TNBC patient-derived xenograft tumor cells.
source: We compared mass spectrometry proteomic profiling of clustering and non-clustering TNBC patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) tumor cells and identified CD81, a tetraspanin protein enriched in extracellular vesicles (EVs) (Kowal et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2021), as one of the altered proteins upon CD44 depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry proteomic profiling data comparing clustering and non-clustering TNBC PDX tumor cells, as stated in the manuscript text.

claim: CD81 is a tetraspanin protein enriched in extracellular vesicles.
source: We compared mass spectrometry proteomic profiling of clustering and non-clustering TNBC patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) tumor cells and identified CD81, a tetraspanin protein enriched in extracellular vesicles (EVs) (Kowal et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2021), as one of the altered proteins upon CD44 depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kowal et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2021) that characterize CD81 as a tetraspanin protein enriched in EVs.

claim: CD44 mediates homophilic interactions for CTC cluster formation as a mechanism to promote self-renewal and polyclonal metastasis in TNBC.
source: CD44 mediates homophilic interactions for CTC cluster formation as a mechanism to promote self-renewal (mammosphere formation) and polyclonal metastasis in TNBC (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2019) demonstrating CD44's role in CTC cluster formation and metastasis.

claim: CD44KO, CD81KO, and dKO MDA-MB-231 cells show diminished capability for mammosphere formation compared to WT controls.
source: In comparison to the WT MDA-MB-231 cells, pooled populations of CD44KO, CD81KO, and dKO cells show similar, diminished capability for mammosphere formation, with fewer and smaller spheres where the dKO did not show much additional effects than single KOs (Figure 1A, B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B, which demonstrate mammosphere formation assays comparing WT, CD44KO, CD81KO, and dKO cells.

claim: Cd81KO 4T1 cells displayed fewer mammospheres compared to WT cells.
source: we also created pooled Cd81KO populations in mouse 4T1 TNBC cells which displayed fewer mammospheres compared to the WT cells, after being seeded with a low number of cells in stem cell medium in suspension, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F demonstrating mammosphere formation in mouse 4T1 cells.

claim: CD81KO and Cd81KO cells showed slightly less confluency compared to respective WT cells.
source: Both CD81KO and Cd81KO cells showed a slightly less confluency compared to respective WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by IncuCyte time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B measuring cell confluence over time.

claim: CD81 KO populations decreased protein levels of breast tumor-initiating markers including OCT4, NOTCH1, and phosphoSTAT3.
source: Like CD44KO cells, CD81 KO populations decreased protein levels of breast tumor-initiating markers including OCT4, NOTCH1, and phosphoSTAT3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C measuring protein expression levels.

claim: CD44 was observed mostly on the cytoplasmic membrane in WT MDA-MB-231 cells, both adherent and in suspension.
source: CD44 was observed mostly on the cytoplasmic membrane in WT MDA-MB-231 cells, both adherent and in suspension, but the intracellular CD44 accumulated specifically in the cells in suspension (p = 0.03) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1C,D with statistical analysis (p = 0.03).

claim: Approximately 50% of adherent cells and 70% of suspension cells showed an average of 14–16% of partial colocalization between CD44 and CD81 on the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: In the WT group, ~50% of adherent cells and 70% of suspension cells showed an average of 14–16% of partial colocalization between CD44 and CD81 on the cytoplasmic membrane, with CD81 mainly presented at the interface of the clustered tumor cells in suspension (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The hotspot residues predicted to be involved in CD44-CD81 interactions are located in domains I and II of CD44 and the extracellular loop of CD81.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, the hotspot residues in warm colors (red and yellow) predicted to be involved in the interactions are located in domains I and II of CD44, which also contribute to CD44–CD44 homophilic interactions (Liu et al., 2019; Kawaguchi et al., 2020), and the extracellular loop of CD81, which links its third and fourth transmembrane domains, with an estimated free energy of binding at −12.23 kcal/mol.
evidence: The claim is supported by machine learning-based protein structure modeling using iTasser, ClusPro, and BAL, with results shown in Figure 1E and citations to previous work (Liu et al., 2019; Kawaguchi et al., 2020).

claim: The estimated free energy of binding between CD44 and CD81 is −12.23 kcal/mol.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, the hotspot residues in warm colors (red and yellow) predicted to be involved in the interactions are located in domains I and II of CD44, which also contribute to CD44–CD44 homophilic interactions (Liu et al., 2019; Kawaguchi et al., 2020), and the extracellular loop of CD81, which links its third and fourth transmembrane domains, with an estimated free energy of binding at −12.23 kcal/mol.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling predictions using BAL shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Endogenous CD81 and CD44 proteins were simultaneously observed within a membrane–fraction protein complex from the lysates of TN1 PDXs and MDA-MB-231 cells, but not CD44KO cells.
source: As expected, after being immunoprecipitated (IP) by anti-CD44 antibody, the endogenous CD81 and CD44 proteins were simultaneously observed within a membrane–fraction protein complex from the lysates of TN1 PDXs (expressing CD44v) and MDA-MB-231 cells (expressing CD44s), but not CD44KO cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Both CD44-Flag and CD81-HA were detected in the protein complex after co-IP with anti-Flag magnetic beads in HEK293T cells.
source: Both CD44-Flag and CD81-HA were detected in the protein complex after co-IP with anti-Flag magnetic beads (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), demonstrating the interaction of exogenous CD44 and CD81 in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E using overexpressed tagged proteins.

claim: CD81d deletion mutant dramatically impairs the interaction with CD44, with an estimated free energy of binding altered to −9.41 kcal/mol.
source: According to predicted protein structures for CD81 and CD44 interactions, we further designed a deletion mutant of CD81d by removing the loop region of amino acids 159–187 (CD81d), which expression was stable and presented on the cell membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), and predicted to dramatically impair the interaction, with an estimated free energy of binding altered to −9.41 kcal/mol (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling predictions shown in Figure 1G and experimental validation of CD81d expression shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: CD81d and CD44.m2 mutant partially lost their capability to interact with CD44 and CD81, respectively.
source: By three independent co-IP tests using the CD44-Flag (WT or mutant) and CD81-HA (WT or mutant) co-transfected cells, we found that CD81d and CD44.m2 mutant partially lost their capability to interact with CD44 and CD81, respectively (Figure 1H)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experimental data from three independent tests shown in Figure 1H.

claim: CD81 reintroduction in CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells rescued mammosphere formation capacity to levels comparable to WT cells.
source: To determine if CD81 reintroduction rescues mammosphere formation, CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells were overexpressed with CD81 (HA/GFP tagged) and assessed for mammosphere formation which yielded comparable capacity to WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by mammosphere formation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H,I using CD81 overexpression rescue experiments.

claim: HA-CD81d mutant overexpression in CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells significantly compromised mammosphere formation capacity.
source: Notably, when HA-CD81d mutant was overexpressed in CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells, mammosphere formation capacity was significantly compromised (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H), suggesting CD81 binding with CD44 is important for functions of self-renewal as measured by mammosphere formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by mammosphere formation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H using CD81d mutant overexpression.

claim: Endocytosis, lysosome, and proteosome pathways are part of the top signature components distinctly altered in siCD81- and siCD44-transfected cells.
source: Most notably, endocytosis, lysosome, and proteosome pathways became part of the top signature components of G2, G4, and G5 clusters distinctly altered in siCD81- and siCD44-transfected cells (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by global mass spectrometry analysis and KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Endocytosis was the top altered pathway within four out of six phosphoproteome clusters (P2, P3, P5, and P6).
source: Interestingly, the alterations in endocytosis pathway components became more evident when phosphoproteome data were analyzed among three groups of cell lysates. Endocytosis was the top altered pathway within four out of six phosphoproteome clusters (P2, P3, P5, and P6), covering both shared and distinct signaling components altered by siCD44 and siCD81.
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphoproteomic mass spectrometry analysis and KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Both siCD44 and siCD81 KDs promoted phosphorylation in the same residues of RAB11FP1, RAB11FP5, EPN2, and SNX12.
source: For example, both KDs promoted phosphorylation in the same residues of RAB11FP1, RAB11FP5, EPN2, and SNX12; siCD44 specifically downregulated phosphorylation in RAB8A and PLD2 but upregulated phosphorylation in GBF1, VPS26A, SNX4, RAB11FIP1, RAB11FIP5; whereas siCD81 downregulated phosphorylation in CAV2, ARFGAP1, and RAB11FIP5 (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D, Supplementary file 5, and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphoproteomic mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C,D and supplementary figures.

claim: CDK1, CDK2, and EGFR are top candidate upstream kinases potentially responsible for siCD81- and siCD44-induced alterations in phosphoproteome clusters.
source: By combining 11 algorithms for machine learning-based kinase prediction, we identified the top candidates of upstream kinases potentially responsible for siCD81- and siCD44-induced alterations in phosphoproteome clusters (P1–P6), especially shared Cluster 4 with decreased phosphopeptides catalyzed by CDK1, CDK2, and EGFR, and Cluster P3 with upregulated phosphorylation by CSNK2A1 (Casein Kinase 2 α1 subunit) in (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by machine learning-based kinase prediction analysis using 11 algorithms, with results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: RAB11FIP1, RAB7A, RAB8A, and RAB10 proteins were validated at elevated levels in CD81KO and CD44KO MDA-MB-231 cells compared to WT cells.
source: RAB11FIP1, RAB7A, RAB8A, and RAB10 proteins were also validated via immunoblot analysis as targets from the proteomic screens and confirmed at elevated levels in CD81KO and CD44KO MDA-MB-231 cells compared to WT cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot validation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C confirming mass spectrometry findings.

claim: GO Localization analysis of downregulated proteins in CD44KO cells revealed the top hits of altered proteins in extracellular exosome/vesicle/organelle.
source: From an independent proteome study using the LC/MS/MS profiles of adherent MDA-MB-231 cells, the GO Processes analysis of upregulated proteins in CD44KO cells indicates regulation of proteolysis and exocytosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 8), whereas the GO Localization analysis of the downregulated proteins in CD44KO cells revealed the top hits of altered proteins in extracellular exosome/vesicle/organelle, previously unknown to be associated with CD44 functions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by GO Localization analysis of mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CD44KO and CD81KO cells have enlarged multivesicular bodies, increased vacuoles, and altered lysosomes compared to WT MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Using ultra-high resolution transmission electron microscopy, we discovered enlarged multivesicular bodies (accumulated endosomes), increased vacuoles (early endosomes or endocytic vesicles), and altered lysosomes in both CD44KO and CD81KO cells in comparison to WT control of MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CD81KO and CD44KO cells secreted a higher number of EVs (particles per cell) to the culture supernatants than the WT cells.
source: CD81KO and CD44KO cells secreted a higher number of EVs (particles per cell) to the culture supernatants than the WT cells, as directly measured by the microflow vesiclometry (MFV) (El-Shennawy et al., 2020; Kibria et al., 2016) or by nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) on NanoSight after EV purification via 100,000 × g ultracentrifugation (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microflow vesiclometry and nanoparticle tracking analysis data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E, with citations to methods (El-Shennawy et al., 2020; Kibria et al., 2016).

claim: The purified EVs (ev44KO and ev81KO) were deficient for both CD44 and CD81 while they showed similar sizes to the WT control with similar EV protein markers such as TSG101 and LAMP2b.
source: The purified EVs (ev44KO and ev81KO) were deficient for both CD44 and CD81 while they showed similar sizes to the WT control with similar EV protein markers such as TSG101 and LAMP2b (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by NTA size distribution analysis and immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: ev81KO displayed impaired membrane integrity.
source: However, when examined by cryo-EM, ev81KO displayed impaired membrane integrity (Figure 3G,H), indicating an essential role for CD81 in modulating EV biogenesis and packaging of membrane proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM imaging data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified 26 out of 416 exosomal proteins differentially expressed in ev44KO, including relatively decreased CD81 and syntenin-1 as well as upregulation of RAB-11B.
source: A mass spectrometry analysis of the ev44WT and ev44KO identified 26 out of 416 exosomal proteins differentially expressed in ev44KO, including relatively decreased CD81 and syntenin-1 as well as upregulation of RAB-11B in association with exosome biogenesis (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of EVs with data provided in Supplementary file 9.

claim: CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells educated by evWT formed larger mammospheres with elevated protein levels of OCT4, pSTAT3, and FAK compared to cells treated with PBS, ev44KO, or ev81KO.
source: The cells educated by evWT formed larger mammospheres with elevated protein levels of OCT4, pSTAT3, and FAK than the cells treated with PBS, ev44KO, or ev81KO (Figure 3J,K, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), demonstrating that EV-presented proteins CD44 and CD81 are required to promote self-renewal of recipient cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by mammosphere formation assay and immunoblot data shown in Figure 3J,K and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A from EV education experiments.

claim: Cd81KO 4T1 cells restored mammosphere formation after exosome education with evWT whereas no rescue effects were observed from ev81KO.
source: Consistently, the Cd81KO 4T1 cells restored mammosphere formation after exosome education with evWT whereas no rescue effects were observed from ev81KO isolated from 4T1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C), demonstrating Cd81-dependent regulation of self-renewal induced by mouse TNBC-secreted EVs.
evidence: The claim is supported by mammosphere formation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B,C using mouse 4T1 cells and EV education.

claim: High expression of CD81 protein in breast tumors was associated with an unfavorable overall survival, relapse-free survival, and distant metastasis-free survival in patients with TNBC.
source: Public database analyses revealed that high expression of CD81 protein in breast tumors was associated with an unfavorable overall survival, relapse-free survival, and distant metastasis-free survival in patients with TNBC (Liu_2014 cohort) (Osz et al., 2021; Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis from public database (Liu_2014 cohort) shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citation to Osz et al., 2021.

claim: A correlation of CD44 and CD81 expression was observed across tumor subtypes (TNBC, HER2, luminal A/B) in a primary breast tumor tissue microarray study.
source: We also conducted a primary breast tumor tissue microarray (TMA) study and observed a correlation of CD44 and CD81 expression across tumor subtypes (TNBC, HER2, luminal A/B) as well as an upregulated expression of CD44/CD81 in TNBC in comparison to luminal A/B (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining and analysis of tumor tissue microarray shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: CD81 expression was detected in over 90% of CTC events (N = 6 patients with 381 CTC events) and 100% of CTC clusters (N = two patients with 10 clusters) using CellSearch platform.
source: CellSearch-based analyses of patient blood samples revealed CD81 expression in over 90% of CTC events (N = 6 patients with 381 CTC events) (Figure 4D,E) and 100% of CTC clusters (N = two patients with 10 clusters).
evidence: The claim is supported by CellSearch immunofluorescence staining data from patient blood samples shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Flow cytometry-based analyses of putative CTCs showed significantly higher expression of CD81 and CD81/CD44 double-positive expression on clusters compared to single cells (N = 50 patients, p = 0.0005).
source: Consistently, flow cytometry-based analyses of putative CTCs (lineage−CD45−EpCAM+/−) and CTC clusters showed a significant higher expression of CD81 and CD81/CD44 double-positive expression on the clusters compared to single cells (N = 50 patients, p = 0.0005) (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis of patient blood samples (N = 50 patients) shown in Figure 4F–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, with statistical significance (p = 0.0005).

claim: Elevated CD81 expression was found in CTC clusters compared to single CTCs using publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets.
source: Using publicly available datasets on single-cell RNA sequencing of Parsotix-filtered CTCs from the blood of patients with breast cancer (Gkountela et al., 2019; Aceto et al., 2014), we also found elevated CD81 expression in CTC clusters compared to single CTCs, confirming the clinical relevance of CD81 as a possible biomarker in CTC clusters and breast cancer metastasis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing data (Gkountela et al., 2019; Aceto et al., 2014) shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: CD81 depletion or downregulation resulted in compromised cluster formation in TN1 and TN2 PDX tumor cells, MDA-MB-231 cells, and 4T1 cells.
source: To further determine the role of CD81 in CTC clustering, we utilized TN1 and TN2 PDX tumor cells, MDA-MB-231 cells, and 4T1 cells to analyze the phenotypic changes caused by siCD81/siCd81-mediated downregulation or CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene depletion. CD81 depletion or downregulation resulted in compromised cluster formation in all four tested human and mouse TNBC models (Figure 4I,J, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by IncuCyte clustering assay data shown in Figure 4I,J and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–C using multiple TNBC models.

claim: CD81 reintroduction in CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells restored tumor clustering close to WT cells, whereas HACD81d mutant failed to do so.
source: To determine if CD81 reintroduction rescues tumor cluster formation, we also assessed the clustering efficiency of CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells when overexpressed with CD81 (HA tagged) which restored tumor clustering close to WT cells, whereas HACD81d mutant failed to do so (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D), suggesting CD81 binding with CD44 is important for functions of tumor cluster formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by IncuCyte clustering assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4D using CD81 overexpression rescue experiments.

claim: An anti-CD81 activating agonist promoted breast tumor cell clustering in a CD81- and CD44-dependent manner.
source: Consistently, an anti-CD81 activating agonist promoted breast tumor cell clustering in a CD81- and CD44-dependent manner as the cluster-enhancing effects of the antibody diminished in both CD81KO and CD44KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E)
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering assay data using anti-CD81 activating antibody shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E.

claim: CD81KO and CD44KO cells showed much more similar and more dramatic reduction in cell invasion compared to migration.
source: In addition, we performed a scratch wound assay with and without Matrigel coverage to evaluate cell invasion and migration, respectively. While CD81KO tumor cells closed the wound at a slightly slower migration speed in the absence of Matrigel compared to that of the WT control, both CD81KO cells and CD44KO cells showed much more similar and more dramatic reduction in cell invasion (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by scratch wound assay data with and without Matrigel shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: CD81− TN1 PDX tumor cells showed compromised tumor initiation and growth compared to CD81+ cells, especially at the 100 cell dilution.
source: After dissociation, CD81+ and CD81− TN1 PDX tumor cells were sorted on a fluorescence-activated cell sorter and then injected at dilutions of 1000 and 100 cells per injection into the mammary fat pads of NSG mice (n = 4 injections/group). Up to 45 days after injection, we observed compromised tumor initiation and growth in the CD81− cells, especially at the 100 cell dilution, compared to the CD81+ cells that grew tumors at both dilutions (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumorigenesis assay data shown in Figure 5A–C using sorted TN1 PDX cells.

claim: Cd81KO 4T1 cells had compromised tumorigenesis compared to WT controls when injected at 1000 and 100 cells per mouse mammary fat pad.
source: Similar tumorigenesis data were observed in Cd81KO 4T1 cells following 1000 and 100 cell injections (Figure 5D,E) (n = 8 injections/group).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumorigenesis assay data shown in Figure 5D,E using mouse 4T1 cells.

claim: CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells had compromised tumor growth and tumorigenesis compared to WT controls when orthotopically implanted at 100 and 10 cells per mouse mammary fat pad injection.
source: Furthermore, CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells had compromised tumor growth (weight) and tumorigenesis compared to WT controls when orthotopically implanted at 100 and 10 cells per mouse mammary fat pad injection (Figure 5F,G) (n = 8 injections/group).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumorigenesis assay data shown in Figure 5F,G using human MDA-MB-231 cells.

claim: CD81 stable overexpression in CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells rescued tumorigenesis and tumor growth.
source: When CD81 was stably overexpressed in CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells tumorigenesis and tumor growth was rescued (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tumorigenesis rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Cd81KO 4T1 tumor cells failed to metastasize to the lungs, with a significantly lower number of metastatic colonies than those of WT tumors.
source: Considering a slightly decreased tumor growth rate in mouse Cd81KO 4T1 cells, we implanted 1000 WT cells and 6000 Cd81KO 4T1 cells into the mammary fat pads of Balb/c mice to achieve comparable tumor burden on day 52 when tumors and lungs were harvested (Figure 6A,B) (n = 5 mice/group; 2 injections/mouse). While there were no significant differences in breast tumor weight between the two groups, Cd81KO tumor cells failed to metastasize to the lungs, with a significantly lower number of metastatic colonies than those of WT tumors (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo spontaneous metastasis assay data shown in Figure 6A–C using mouse 4T1 cells.

claim: Mice bearing Cd81KO 4T1 tumors had 100% survival compared to 0% survival of the mice with oversized WT tumors by day 52.
source: Furthermore, the mice bearing Cd81KO tumors had 100% survival compared to 0% survival of the mice with oversized WT tumors by day 52 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 6D from the spontaneous metastasis experiment.

claim: CD81KO MDA-MB-231 cells phenocopied CD44KO cells with impaired or lost capability to develop spontaneous lung metastases in mice after being normalized by tumor burden.
source: Furthermore, when human TNBC cells were implanted orthotopically at 10,000 cells to ensure tumor growth, CD81KO cells phenocopied CD44KO cells with impaired or lost capability to develop spontaneous lung metastases in mice after being normalized by tumor burden (Figure 6E–H) (n = 5 mice/group; 2 injections/mouse)
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo spontaneous metastasis assay data shown in Figure 6E–H using human MDA-MB-231 cells.

claim: Mice bearing CD81KO or CD44KO MDA-MB-231 tumors had significantly better survival than those bearing WT tumors.
source: Furthermore, when human TNBC cells were implanted orthotopically at 10,000 cells to ensure tumor growth, CD81KO cells phenocopied CD44KO cells with impaired or lost capability to develop spontaneous lung metastases in mice after being normalized by tumor burden (Figure 6E–H) (n = 5 mice/group; 2 injections/mouse), resulting in a significantly better survival of the mice bearing KO tumors than those bearing WT tumors (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 6I from the spontaneous metastasis experiment.

claim: Diminished lung colonization was observed in NSG mice 26 days after receiving CD81KO cells in comparison with WT cells via tail vein injection.
source: Consistently, diminished lung colonization or experimental metastasis were observed in the NSG mice 26 days after receiving CD81KO cells in comparison with that of WT cells via tail vein injection, as measured via bioluminescence imaging, fluorescence microscopy, and HE-staining of lung tissues (Figure 6J–L, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) (n = 3 mice/group).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental metastasis assay data shown in Figure 6J–L and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A using tail vein injection.

claim: siCD81 transfection-mediated transient KD of CD81 reduced the metastatic potential of MDA-MB-231 cells following tail vein injection.
source: Meanwhile, siCD81 transfection-mediated transient KD of CD81 also reduced the metastatic potential of MDA-MB-231 cells following tail vein injection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C) (n = 3 mice/group).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental metastasis assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C using siCD81 knockdown.

claim: Cd81 KO 4T1 cells (singles and clusters) were less detectable in the blood than WT controls within 1 day following tail vein injection, in parallel with reduced seeding for lung colonization.
source: Finally, we measured the CTC events in the blood within 1 day following tail vein injection of 4T1 tumor cells and found that Cd81 KO cells (singles and clusters) were less detectable than the WT controls, in parallel with reduced seeding for lung colonization (Figure 6M–O) (n = 3 mice/group).
evidence: The claim is supported by CTC detection and lung colonization data shown in Figure 6M–O from tail vein injection experiments.

claim: CD81 is a novel partner interacting with CD44 in breast tumor-initiating cells.
source: In a summary, CD81 is a novel partner interacting with CD44 in breast tumor-initiating cells and promotes exosome-induced self-renewal (mammosphere formation and signature markers), tumor cluster formation, and therefore enhancing tumor initiation and lung metastasis of TNBC with an unfavorable overall survival and metastasis-free survival (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript, with a schematic shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: CD81 promotes exosome-induced self-renewal, tumor cluster formation, and enhances tumor initiation and lung metastasis of TNBC.
source: In a summary, CD81 is a novel partner interacting with CD44 in breast tumor-initiating cells and promotes exosome-induced self-renewal (mammosphere formation and signature markers), tumor cluster formation, and therefore enhancing tumor initiation and lung metastasis of TNBC with an unfavorable overall survival and metastasis-free survival (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript, with a schematic shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: CD81 function in cancer metastasis is tumor cell intrinsic and can be independent of adaptive immunity.
source: While CD81 function has primarily been studied in immune cells (Vences-Catalán et al., 2015; Maecker and Levy, 1997; Quast et al., 2011; van Zelm et al., 2010), this newly identified function of CD81 in cancer metastasis is tumor cell intrinsic and can be independent of adaptive immunity, as shown in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from both immunocompetent (Balb/c) and immunocompromised (NSG) mice, with citations to previous work on CD81 in immune cells (Vences-Catalán et al., 2015; Maecker and Levy, 1997; Quast et al., 2011; van Zelm et al., 2010).

claim: Tetraspanin proteins make up tetraspanin enriched microdomains that are crucial in regulating the motility and interactions of cancer cells with their microenvironment.
source: Tetraspanin proteins, such as CD81, are best known for making up tetraspanin enriched microdomains (Zöller, 2009; Le Naour et al., 2006). These microdomains are crucial in regulating the motility and interactions of cancer cells with their microenvironment by organizing other transmembrane proteins, such as cell adhesion molecules, growth factors, and proteases (Zöller, 2009; Le Naour et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zöller, 2009; Le Naour et al., 2006) describing tetraspanin protein functions.

claim: CD44 was observed among the EV protein interactome network pulled down by CD81 peptides in a study by Perez-Hernandez et al.
source: A study by Perez-Hernandez et al. also observed CD44 among the EV protein interactome network pulled down by CD81 peptides without exploring their relevance to EV functions (Perez-Hernandez et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Perez-Hernandez et al., 2013) that identified CD44 in CD81 interactome.

claim: TSPAN8 and CD9 may promote cancer self-renewal in colorectal cancer and glioblastoma, respectively.
source: Nevertheless, other tetraspanin proteins, such as TSPAN8 and CD9, may promote cancer self-renewal in colorectal cancer (Zhu et al., 2019) and glioblastoma (Podergajs et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zhu et al., 2019; Podergajs et al., 2016) on other tetraspanin proteins.

claim: A potential anti-CD81 therapeutic strategy was identified to block the pro-metastatic effect of CD81 in animal studies.
source: A potential anti-CD81 therapeutic strategy was identified to block the pro-metastatic effect of CD81 in animal studies (Vences-Catalán et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work (Vences-Catalán et al., 2021) on anti-CD81 therapeutic strategy.

claim: CD44 is a multifunctional class I transmembrane glycoprotein and is widely used as a marker of breast tumor-initiating cells, especially in TNBC.
source: CD44 is a multifunctional class I transmembrane glycoprotein and is widely used as a marker of breast tumor-initiating cells, especially in TNBC (Idowu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Idowu et al., 2012) and established scientific knowledge about CD44.

claim: CD44 and CD81 interactions on the cell membrane might provide feedback for protein networks and modifications.
source: CD44 and CD81 interactions on the cell membrane might provide feedback for protein networks and modifications.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the observed interactions and functional relationships between CD44 and CD81.

claim: A transmembrane ubiquitin ligase family member MARCH8 has been associated with lysosome degradation of both CD44 and CD81 in fibroblast cells and/or TNBC cells.
source: Notably, a transmembrane ubiquitin ligase family member MARCH8 has been associated with lysosome degradation of both CD44 and CD81 in fibroblast cells (Bartee et al., 2010) and/or TNBC cells (Chen et al., 2021), suggesting CD44 and CD81 might follow similar fates of protein degradation or recycling in both cancer cells and other cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bartee et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2021) on MARCH8 function.

claim: Tumor recurrence often occurs due to an increased number of CTCs, some of which display tumor-regenerative plasticity and reprogramming phenotypes.
source: Several studies suggest tumor recurrence often occurs due to an increased number of CTCs, some of which display tumor-regenerative plasticity and reprogramming phenotypes (Giordano et al., 2012; Książkiewicz et al., 2012; Aktas et al., 2009), or transform into tumor-initiating cells (Dahan et al., 2014; Dawood et al., 2014; Giuliano et al., 2011; Pierga et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Giordano et al., 2012; Książkiewicz et al., 2012; Aktas et al., 2009; Dahan et al., 2014; Dawood et al., 2014; Giuliano et al., 2011; Pierga et al., 2012).

claim: Cancer exosomes can be part of the transforming factors upon uptake by CTCs.
source: Our studies demonstrated that cancer exosomes can be part of the transforming factors upon uptake by the CTCs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the EV education experiments showing that exosomes can promote self-renewal in recipient cells.

claim: A CD44 variant has been reported to be involved in interluminal vesicle loading.
source: While CD44 remains understudied in exosome biogenesis, a CD44 variant has been reported to be involved in interluminal vesicle loading (Wang et al., 2018) which may be linked to maintaining tumor-initiating cells and tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work (Wang et al., 2018) on CD44 variant function in vesicle loading.

claim: A subset of CTCs and tumor-initiating cells may exhibit dynamic changes in epithelial–mesenchymal transition phenotype.
source: Furthermore, a subset of CTCs and tumor-initiating cells may exhibit dynamic changes in epithelial–mesenchymal transition phenotype (Yu et al., 2013), which can upregulate CD81 expression in mesenchymal breast cancer (Uretmen Kagiali et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Yu et al., 2013; Uretmen Kagiali et al., 2019) on EMT and CD81 expression.

claim: CD81+/CD56+/CD45− markers have been used to detect neuroblastoma cells in the peripheral blood of patients.
source: While the role of CD81 displayed on CTCs is largely understudied, previous studies have used CD81+/CD56+/CD45− markers to detect neuroblastoma cells in the peripheral blood of patients (Nagai et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work (Nagai et al., 2000) on CD81 as a marker for neuroblastoma cells.

claim: Breast cancer killed nearly 0.7 million people worldwide in 2020 with metastasis accounting for 90% of deaths.
source: Breast cancer killed nearly 0.7 million people worldwide in 2020 with metastasis accounting for 90% of deaths (Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published epidemiological data (Sung et al., 2021).

claim: Triple negative breast cancer comprises 10–15% of newly diagnosed breast cancer cases and is highly metastatic with low long-term survival.
source: Negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 amplification, triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) comprises 10–15% of newly diagnosed breast cancer cases and is highly metastatic with low long-term survival (Perou et al., 2000; Sørlie et al., 2001; Rakha et al., 2007; Haffty et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Perou et al., 2000; Sørlie et al., 2001; Rakha et al., 2007; Haffty et al., 2006) on TNBC characteristics.

claim: TNBC preferentially metastasizes to the visceral organs such as the lungs, liver, and brain.
source: TNBC preferentially metastasizes to the visceral organs such as the lungs, liver, and brain (Foulkes et al., 2010; Dent et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Foulkes et al., 2010; Dent et al., 2007) on TNBC metastasis patterns.

claim: Tumor-initiating cells with self-renewal and regenerative reprogramming capacity are the underlying cause of cancer relapse, therapy resistance, and distant dissemination.
source: Growing evidence suggests tumor-initiating cells, or cancer stem cells with self-renewal and regenerative reprogramming capacity, are the underlying cause of cancer relapse, therapy resistance, and distant dissemination (Diehn et al., 2009; Li et al., 2008; Al-Hajj et al., 2003; Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2010; Giordano et al., 2013; Idowu et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2012; Owens and Naylor, 2013; Liu et al., 2010; Liu and Wicha, 2010; Korkaya and Wicha, 2009; Adorno-Cruz et al., 2015; Ramos et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies on tumor-initiating cells and cancer stem cells.

claim: Tumor-initiating cells have measurable clinical impact on patient outcomes.
source: Growing evidence suggests tumor-initiating cells, or cancer stem cells with self-renewal and regenerative reprogramming capacity, are the underlying cause of cancer relapse, therapy resistance, and distant dissemination (Diehn et al., 2009; Li et al., 2008; Al-Hajj et al., 2003; Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2010; Giordano et al., 2013; Idowu et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2012; Owens and Naylor, 2013; Liu et al., 2010; Liu and Wicha, 2010; Korkaya and Wicha, 2009; Adorno-Cruz et al., 2015; Ramos et al., 2017) with measurable clinical impact on patient outcomes (Liu et al., 2010; Bhola et al., 2013; Calcagno et al., 2010; Phillips et al., 2006; Creighton et al., 2009; Shats et al., 2011; Lathia et al., 2020; Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008; Idowu et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2012; Owens and Naylor, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies on clinical impact of tumor-initiating cells.

claim: Machine learning and deep learning have transformed protein structure modeling and greatly facilitated the understanding of molecular networks and therapeutic development.
source: Among the biomolecular mechanisms, protein functions, and their networks are the backbones directly related to cellular phenotype and performance. Machine learning and deep learning have transformed protein structure modeling and greatly facilitated the understanding of molecular networks and therapeutic development (Karimi et al., 2020; AlQuraishi, 2021; Baek and Baker, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Karimi et al., 2020; AlQuraishi, 2021; Baek and Baker, 2022) on machine learning applications in protein structure modeling.

claim: CTCs with genetic and/or epigenetic alterations are tumor cells that shed from cancer lesions and circulate within the blood or lymphatic vasculature before seeding with a very low frequency to distant organs for metastatic tumor regeneration.
source: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) with genetic and/or epigenetic alterations (Fernandez et al., 2014; Gkountela et al., 2019) are tumor cells that shed from cancer lesions and circulate within the blood or lymphatic vasculature before seeding with a very low frequency to distant organs for metastatic tumor regeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fernandez et al., 2014; Gkountela et al., 2019) on CTC characteristics.

claim: Detection of CTC events on the CellSearch platform is associated with patient outcomes in which multicellular CTC clusters predict worse prognosis and mediate metastasis in a 20- to 100-fold higher efficiency than single CTCs.
source: Detection of CTC events on the CellSearch platform is associated with patient outcomes in which multicellular CTC clusters predict worse prognosis and mediate metastasis in a 20- to 100-fold higher efficiency than single CTCs (Mu et al., 2015; Aceto et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mu et al., 2015; Aceto et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019) on CTC clusters and patient outcomes.

claim: CD44 is highly enriched in CTC clusters and predicts an unfavorable overall survival of patients with breast cancer, especially TNBC.
source: Our recent work demonstrated that the breast tumor-initiating cell marker CD44 is highly enriched in CTC clusters and predicts an unfavorable overall survival of patients with breast cancer, especially TNBC (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2019) on CD44 in CTC clusters.

claim: Most of cell-secreted EVs are characterized by presence of membrane structure, enriched protein markers such as CD81, CD63, CD9, and TSG101, and other components like lipids, nucleic acids, and metabolites.
source: Most of cell-secreted EVs (30–1000 nm), if not all, are characterized by presence of membrane structure, enriched protein markers such as CD81, CD63, CD9, and TSG101, and other components like lipids, nucleic acids, and metabolites (Kowal et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2021; Bobrie et al., 2011; Théry et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kowal et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2021; Bobrie et al., 2011; Théry et al., 2006) on EV characteristics.

claim: The biogenesis pathway of large EVs via plasma membrane shedding is distinct from that of small EVs generated from the invagination of the plasma membrane to form endosomes.
source: The biogenesis pathway of large EVs (such as microvesicles) via plasma membrane shedding is distinct from that of small EVs (such as exosomes). The latter is generated from the invagination of the plasma membrane to form endosomes that continue to invaginate and mature into multivesicular bodies destined for either lysosome degradation or fusion with the plasma membrane and release as exosomes (Bobrie et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Bobrie et al., 2011) on EV biogenesis pathways.

claim: EVs have emerged as key players in intercellular communications in both physiological and pathological settings, including cancer development and distant organ-specific metastasis.
source: EVs have emerged as key players in intercellular communications in both physiological and pathological settings, including cancer development (Iero et al., 2008; Kahlert and Kalluri, 2013) and distant organ-specific metastasis (Hoshino et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Iero et al., 2008; Kahlert and Kalluri, 2013; Hoshino et al., 2015) on EV functions.
